name: Coolors
tagline: A fast color palette generator with locking, contrast checking, and export to code or design tools.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core loop here is generate five colors, lock the ones you like, hit space, repeat. That is a few hundred lines of code plus a decent color space library, and any competent agent will get you there in an afternoon. The genuinely useful extras, contrast ratios, shade ramps, hex/HSL/OKLCH readouts, CSS variable export, are all deterministic math you can ask for in the same prompt. What you cannot rebuild is the community palette feed and the twelve years of SEO that makes Coolors the default answer to "nice color combos". If you mostly hit spacebar until something looks right, a local build covers it.
coreLoopDIY: A browser page that generates harmonious palettes with per-swatch locking and spacebar regeneration, then exports them as CSS variables, Tailwind config, or JSON.
requirements: Node for local dev, or just a single static HTML file if you want zero tooling
whatYouLose: The explore feed of community palettes, which is the part people actually browse for inspiration
Image color extraction and the gradient/contrast side tools, unless you ask for them explicitly
Mobile apps and offline palette sync across devices
Someone else's taste: naive random generation looks worse than curated palettes until you tune the harmony rules
moatNotes: The generator is commodity. The million-palette library and the habit of typing "coolors" into the address bar are not.
whyPeopleStillPay: Pro is cheap, removes ads, and unlocks the collections and image-picker workflow, which is less friction than maintaining your own tool. Designers also use it as a shared vocabulary: sending a Coolors link is faster than sending a JSON file nobody can open. And most people do not want a palette generator, they want to browse palettes other people already liked, which is a content product wearing a tool's clothes.
notes: One of the few design SaaS products whose main feature is genuinely a weekend afternoon of color math.
prompt:
Build a local color palette generator as a single-page app. No accounts, no backend, no telemetry, no analytics.

Stack: Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind. Use the `culori` package for color conversion and contrast math. Nothing else.

Core UI:
- Full-height row of 5 vertical color panels, each filling equal width. On narrow screens stack them vertically.
- Pressing the spacebar regenerates every unlocked swatch. This is the primary interaction; make it feel instant.
- Each panel shows its hex code, a lock toggle, a copy-hex button, and a delete button. Locked swatches survive regeneration.
- Buttons to add a swatch (max 10) and to remove one (min 2).
- Click a hex code to edit it inline; accept hex, rgb(), or oklch() input.

Generation: do not use pure random RGB. Implement harmony modes in OKLCH: random, analogous, complementary, triadic, split-complementary, and monochromatic. A dropdown picks the mode. Keep lightness and chroma within ranges that look intentional, and spread lightness across the swatches so palettes stay usable for UI.

Extras, all computed locally:
- Per swatch, show WCAG contrast ratio against both white and black, with the AA/AAA pass labels.
- A detail drawer per swatch with a 9-step tint/shade ramp (50 to 900) and click-to-copy on each step.
- Export panel with copy buttons for: CSS custom properties, a Tailwind `colors` object, JSON array, and an SVG swatch strip.

Persistence: current palette in the URL hash as dash-separated hex (so links are shareable), plus a saved-palettes list in localStorage with rename and delete. Undo/redo for the last 20 generations via a keyboard shortcut.

Out of scope: image color extraction, community browsing, user accounts, any network request at runtime.

Ship a README with `npm install`, `npm run dev`, and the keyboard shortcuts. No .env needed since there are no secrets.
